One fixed permutation for three, four and more inputs at small error

On 128 bits, a single explicit permutation sends every ordered quadruple within 2−1282^{-128} of uniform after 129 cipher rounds. The same permutation gives 81 rounds for triples. A second choice gives 225 rounds for eight inputs. Each uses one public table or circuit throughout and independent uniform XOR keys, as in Problem 4. These numbers are sufficient upper bounds.

Bits nn Updated bits bb Tuple order tt Rounds for 2−322^{-32} Rounds for 2−642^{-64} Rounds for 2−1282^{-128}
64 8 3 65 113 209
128 16 3 33 49 81
128 16 4 33 65 129
128 8 8 65 129 225
256 32 4 17 33 65

For all sufficiently large nn and every target 2≤t≤n/2−12\le t\le n/2-1, choosing the block width for that target gives O(t(1+log(1/ϵ)/n))O(t(1+\log(1/\epsilon)/n)) rounds. In particular, at error 2−n2^{-n} the bound is O(t)O(t), matching the key-count lower bound up to a constant. Each public permutation is fixed throughout its run. Its bound for tt also applies to all smaller orders by projection.

Construction and verification

Take 1≤b≤n/21\le b\le n/2, write B=2bB=2^b, N=2nN=2^n, and Q=2n−bQ=2^{n-b}. Split an input into its low bb bits vv and the other bits zz. Interpret zz in a specified polynomial basis of 𝔽Q\mathbb F_Q. Put I(0)=0I(0)=0 and I(z)=1/zI(z)=1/z elsewhere. Let f(z)f(z) be the low bb coordinates of I(z)I(z). Define E(v,z)=(v⊕f(z),z)E(v,z)=(v\oplus f(z),z) and let RR rotate the entire word right by bb positions, moving the low block to the high end. Use the fixed public permutation P0=REP_0=R E. The invertible update EE is an unbalanced Feistel step. Any surjective binary linear projection in place of the low bb coordinates gives the same bound.

The verifier accepts this compact description and checks irreducibility of the field modulus in polynomial time in nn. A generic supplied circuit still needs a witness that it implements this formula. For a table, the verifier compares every entry to P0P_0 and automatically includes the number hh of disagreements. The table check costs O(Npoly(n))O(N\,\mathrm{poly}(n)). The first command verifies both large and small thresholds on the specified compact 128-bit example, whose irreducible modulus is X112+X5+X4+X3+1X^{112}+X^5+X^4+X^3+1. Pass a table with --file to verify a concrete list instead. Verifier

uv run --locked python -m research.spectral_certificate --bits 128 --block-bits 16 --order 4 --modulus 0x10000000000000000000000000039 --error-bits 32 64 128
uv run --locked python -m research.spectral_certificate --bits 128 --block-bits 8 --order 8 --modulus 0x100000000000000000000000000001b

β=2(s−1)Q+s+1Q,η=12Bs−1β,δ=min(1,d(t2)C(B−1)N+2d(η+th/N)). \beta=\frac{2(s-1)\sqrt Q+s+1}{Q},\qquad \eta=\tfrac12\sqrt{B^s-1}\,\beta,\qquad \delta=\min\left(1,\frac{d\binom t2 C(B-1)}{N}+2d(\eta+th/N)\right).

dt(1+2dj)≤δ(2δ)j−1,j≥1.d_t(1+2dj)\le\delta(2\delta)^{j-1},\qquad j\ge1.

Replacing the translated update by independent offsets

In the ideal layer each control zz gets an independent uniform bb-bit offset. A tuple addresses at most ss distinct controls. For any k≤sk\le s distinct controls, Fourier inversion, Parseval and Cauchy–Schwarz give TV at most Bk−1β/2\sqrt{B^k-1}\,\beta/2 if the bias of every nonzero joint binary parity of its kk offsets is at most β\beta. This is a standard small-bias estimate. Naor and Naor

Here is why the needed bias holds for the inverse projection. By nondegeneracy of the field trace pairing, any nontrivial parity uses a nonempty set of j≤kj\le k distinct controls aia_i and nonzero coefficients ci∈𝔽Qc_i\in\mathbb F_Q. Off these controls the parity is the absolute trace of g(u)=∑i=1jciu+ai.g(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{j}\frac{c_i}{u+a_i}. Each pole is simple with nonzero residue, which also ensures the Artin–Schreier curve y2+y=g(u)y^2+y=g(u) is geometrically irreducible. Its smooth projective model has genus j−1j-1. Each finite pole contributes one rational point, and infinity contributes two since g(∞)=0g(\infty)=0. Consequently its point count equals Q+2+∑u∉{ai}(−1)Tr(g(u))Q+2+\sum_{u\notin\{a_i\}}(-1)^{\operatorname{Tr}(g(u))}. Hasse–Weil bounds its distance from Q+1Q+1 by 2(j−1)Q2(j-1)\sqrt Q. Including the jj patched summands changes the sum by at most jj, giving the claimed β\beta. This uses classical arithmetic of Artin–Schreier curves. Bucur, David, Feigon and Lalín, §2

Two sweeps of the ideal updates

Remove the deterministic rotations by tracking coordinates in a rotating frame. A sweep consists of dd updates of successive bb-bit windows. They cover all the coordinates. If bb divides nn they are disjoint. Otherwise only the first and last overlap, in db−ndb-n coordinates.

Track two distinct points. When their controls differ, their two ideal offsets are independent. The difference on the updated window is therefore freshly uniform. When the controls agree, the existing nonzero difference lies entirely within that window and stays fixed. Call this update forced. Among the first d−1d-1 disjoint windows, at most one update can be forced, since it leaves a nonzero difference in an already processed window. In the disjoint case this holds across all dd windows. There are at most two forced updates in the overlapping case.

Fix a candidate final difference. In the disjoint case it determines every written window. Its probability after the sweep is at most B−(d−1)=B/NB^{-(d-1)}=B/N. In the overlapping case there are at most 2db−n2^{db-n} possible first writes on the bits that are subsequently overwritten. Every possible history has probability at most B−(d−2)B^{-(d-2)}. Consequently every nonzero difference has probability at most C/NC/N after one sweep. Each subsequent ideal difference kernel is doubly stochastic. On a nonzero fixed control difference it replaces the window uniformly, and on control difference zero it fixes the nonzero window. Thus the same pointwise upper bound applies throughout the second sweep.

At a given second-sweep step the probability that some two tracked points share a control is at most (t2)(B−1)C/N\binom t2(B-1)C/N, since a colliding difference is one of the B−1B-1 nonzero differences supported in that window. Couple these ideal updates to a process that uses fresh independent offsets for each point, even when two controls match. They can agree throughout the second sweep unless a control collision occurs. The independent process ends in tt independent uniform points, since all coordinates are refreshed by independent uniform window bits. This gives the first term of δ\delta by a union bound. The ideal process always ends in distinct points. For any law supported there, conditioning the independent uniform target on distinctness can only decrease its TV from that law: conditioning increases the target mass at every possible observed point and decreases the total positive excess.

Comparing actual and ideal layers for 2d2d steps costs at most 2d(η+th/N)2d(\eta+th/N) by successive couplings. Thus every row of the 2d2d-step actual kernel is within δ\delta of uniform. The largest TV distance between two rows is at most 2δ2\delta. Decomposing a signed measure into positive and negative parts gives that contraction factor for each subsequent block. Uniform is stationary, proving the bound.

Scaling and prior work

For 2≤t≤n/2−12\le t\le n/2-1, take b=⌊n/(2(t+1))⌋b=\lfloor n/(2(t+1))\rfloor and h=0h=0. Since the floor of a real number at least one is at least half that number, d≤4(t+1)+1d\le4(t+1)+1. The bias contribution is O(t22−(n−b(t+1))/2)=O(t22−n/4)O(t^2 2^{-(n-b(t+1))/2})=O(t^2 2^{-n/4}), and the ideal term is O(t323b−n)=O(t32−n/2)O(t^3 2^{3b-n})=O(t^3 2^{-n/2}). Thus 2δ≤2−n/52\delta\le2^{-n/5} for all sufficiently large nn, uniformly over the stated orders. Taking j=max(1,⌈5log2(1/ϵ)/n⌉)j=\max(1,\lceil5\log_2(1/\epsilon)/n\rceil) proves the round bound. Conversely rr independent nn-bit keys can reach at most NrN^r target tuples. TV at most ϵ\epsilon requires Nr≥(1−ϵ)(N)tN^r\ge(1-\epsilon)(N)_t, where (N)t=N(N−1)⋯(N−t+1)(N)_t=N(N-1)\cdots(N-t+1). At ϵ=2−n\epsilon=2^{-n} this gives r≥tr\ge t for these orders and sufficiently large nn. A different tradeoff uses b=1b=1 to allow t≤(1−γ)nt\le(1-\gamma)n for fixed 0<γ<10<\gamma<1, still obtaining exponentially small block error up to polynomial factors.

Morris, Rogaway and Stegers study precisely the independent-switch one-bit model under the name Thorp shuffle, giving a stronger ideal bound after 2n−12n-1 steps. Hoang and Rogaway treat wider unbalanced Feistel networks in their independent random-function model. Kaplan, Naor and Reingold construct almost tt-wise permutations via derandomization and discuss Feistel networks with richer function families. The local Fourier estimate, character-sum bound and TV amplification are established tools. The particular repeated public inverse-projection construction, its translation reduction, and the stated quantitative guarantee are project derivations whose publication priority is unverified.
